entries.title: UNGA day 4: Lebanon calls for peacekeepers to replace UNIFIL
entries.summary: Lebanon's prime minister has told the UN that the withdrawal of peacekeeping troops risks creating a vacuum. Leaders from Pakistan and Iraq are also speaking on day four of a conference dominated by the Middle East.
entries.content:
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

Lebanon's prime minister has told the UN that the withdrawal of peacekeeping troops risks creating a vacuum. Leaders from Pakistan and Iraq are also speaking on day four of a conference dominated by the Middle East.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • UNGA Day 4 opened with remarks from Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam as well as the prime ministers of Iraq and Pakistan and others
  • Salam called for peacekeepers to remain in his country as Israel operates in a self-declared 'security zone' in south Lebanon
  • The address came one day after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered defiant and controversial remarks on Thursday afternoon
  • The president of Kiribati and the vice president of the Maldives, two island nations acutely threatened by rising sea levels, also addressed the General Assembly on Friday

Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:

Skip next section Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'

Lebanese prime minister says 'the problem is not the absence of rules'

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam told the UN that "without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among states, nor can competition among them flourish."

He said that the UN was founded, more than 80 years ago, on "the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force."

But Salam said that wars and conflicts still plague a world that spends more on armaments than on development.

"The problem is not the absence of rules," Salam said. "It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application."

He did not mention Israel by name in his preamble but did later in his speech. 

Salam said his government had three commitments to fulfil, and argued that all three were interconnected:

  • Restoring trust and credibility in Lebanese authorities after the economic collapse and vast port explosion in Beirut of August 4, 2020
  • Ensuring that only the Lebanese government held weapons and make decisions of war for the country — comments seemingly aimed at the pro-Iranian Hezbollah group, which he did not name 
  • Reclaiming occupied Lebanese territory from Israel under the terms of UN Resolution 1701 adopted to end the Second Lebanon War between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006

"Our position on the war has been clear from the outset," Salam said. "We want it to end. We want the ceasefire consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognized borders, in accordance with the 1949 General Armistice Agreement and as affirmed by Resolution 1701. We want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and a reconstruction of what the war destroyed."

Under the tense ceasefire deal between Lebanon and Israel, brokered by the US, Israel is supposed to withdraw its forces from a self-declared "buffer zone" in southern Lebanon. In turn, Lebanon's government is supposed to move its military fores into these areas and stop Hezbollah from using them to launch attacks into northern Israel. The current goal is to create so-called pilot zones where the Lebanese army moves in and Israel's troops move out. 

The process is making only gradual progress, as both sides accuse the other of failing to meet their obligations.

Skip next section Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends

Lebanon PM calls for peacekeeping troops after UNIFIL mandate ends

Lebanon Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called for the UN to keep its UNIFIL (UN Interim Force in Lebanon) peacekeeping troops in place after their mandate expires at year's end.

"What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it," he said.

The UN's troops, currently numbering 7,500 from 46 different countries, have been in Lebanon since 1978.

Last year, however, the US pushed the UN Security Council to terminate the mandate when it ran out.

UNIFIL's expected departure comes as Israel maintains troops in its own self-declared "security zone" extending some 10 kilometers (6 miles) into south Lebanon.

Skip next section Welcome back to our coverage

Welcome back to our coverage

We are resuming our coverage of the United Nations General Assembly on Friday, September 25.

The general debate is scheduled to begin its fourth day of the assembly at 9 a.m. New York time (1300 UTC).

Iraq, Pakistan, Lebanon and others are to speak in today's morning session, while countries such as Egypt, Mexico, Kazakhstan and Sweden will take the stand in the afternoon.

Friday's debate comes after a day of speeches that was centered on Gaza, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's address sparking a walkout by several delegates.

Skip next section That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

That's a wrap on Day 3 of UNGA

We're wrapping up for the day, with the third day's sessions of the 81st General Assembly now complete.

Gaza dominated the speeches today.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the assembly, denying that his country's actions in Gaza amount to genocide, an accusation leveled by several speakers on Thursday, including Palestinian Prime Minister Mahmoud Abbas.

Several delegates exited the hall as the Israeli prime minister began his speech.

Protesters had also gathered outside the UN Headquarters in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address, with some being arrested.

Before the session wrapped up, the representatives of Iran, Turkey and Qatar used their right of reply to lambast Netanyahu's address.

Join us on Friday, when Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Egypt, Mexico, Haiti, Norway, Sweden and others are due to address the assembly.

Skip next section Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's young prime minister stood at the podium of the UN General Assembly to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," said Balendra Shah as he began his address to the UNGA on Thursday.

Nepal's leader calls for international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas

The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a "Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism," which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster. 

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change

Shah noted that his country only contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he wasn not blaming any nation or continent.

"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.

Nepal seeks grants, not loans, for flood recovery

The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of "Responsibility, Reparation and Resilience" as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.

Shah said that vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

36-year-old Shah was theyoungest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.

Skip next section 'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

'Hands off ICC,' Dutch PM says amid growing US pressure

Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten, addressing the General Assembly on Thursday, said the International Criminal Court, which is based in The Hague, was "under attack."

Jetten did not name the US or President Donald Trump, who on Tuesday urged countries to leave the court, the latest move in his administration's campaign against the ICC.

"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes?" Jetten asked the assembly, drawing loud applause from the delegates.

"I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order. Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity."

Washington has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on ICC staff, with officials reportedly preparing additional sanctions that could curtail the court's ability to operate.

Skip next section Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA

Yemen, Kuwait stress freedom of navigation at UNGA

Yemen and Kuwait, both heavily impacted by the Iran war and its regional spillover, have used their General Assembly addresses to stress the importance of the freedom and safety of navigation, while condemning Iran and its proxies in the region.

Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, vice resident of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, represents the internationally recognized government, which has been at war with the Iran-backed Houthirebels for more than a decade.

Alimi-Bawzer devoted his address to highlighting recent Houthi actions and their impact on global trade.

The Houthis' conflict with Saudi Arabia, which has led a coalition against them, has recently escalated, with the Yemeni rebels declaring a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial global shipping route. This has further squeezed the Saudi kingdom as Iran continues to block access through the Strait of Hormuz.

"Ensuring security at sea begins with eliminating the source of the threat on land," Alimi-Bawzer said, in an apparent reference to the Houthis.

Kuwaiti Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah stressed that freedom and safety of navigation, as well as the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, must be guaranteed.

"To inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz, using it as a bargaining chip in the war, in violation of international law and relevant Security Council resolutions," he said.

Kuwait has been among the countries targeted by Iranian strikes since the start of the war, in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes. 

Skip next section Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'

Nigeria says don't 'surrender our technological future to paranoia'

Nigeria's Vice President Kashim Shettima addressed the assembly on behalf of President Bola Tinubu.

Among a range of issues, he weighed in on the question of AI with an appeal for an optimistic and proactive approach more than what he deemed undue caution.

"We refuse to surrender our technological future to paranoia," he said. "An invention can be destructive or beneficial, depending on the purpose it serves and the judgment of those who use it. A knife can take a life in the hands of an assailant, and can save one in the hands of a surgeon."

He said that while AI could be used to wage war, it could also "transform" an array of areas like healthcare, education and agriculture.

"Much of the anxiety surrounding AI reflects the distrust we have allowed to grow amongst us," Shettima said.

He said Nigeria wished to invite the world "to work with our inventive, resourceful and enterprising young people to direct AI towards humanity's advancement rather than its destruction."

Skip next section Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'

Fiji calls for cheaper financial transfers for remittances, saying 'they are not aid'

Fijian President Ratu Naiqama Tawakecolati Lalabalavu addressed the chamber on behalf of one of the low-lying island nations at severe risk from climate change on Thursday.

He said that many of the UN's sustainable development goals remained off track with 2030 approaching and said that aid and financial assistance often did a poor job of reaching remote islands exposed to more natural disasters than average. But then he called for a wider financial system that would better enable Fijians to help themselves.

"There is one measure of delivery that reaches Fijian households directly," he said. "Remittances are now Fiji's third-largest source of foreign exchange."

Lalabalavu said these funds paid for school fees, rebuilt homes after cyclones and sustained families between harvests.

"Your excellencies, they are not aid. They are earnings of Fijians abroad, sent home. Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive in the world through which to send money."

He noted how the chamber had in May committed to work to keep such transfer costs below 3% and to eliminate corridors costing more than 5% — he said that Pacific countries like Fiji wanted this to be "treated as an obligation and not an aspiration."

"Labor mobility must also not become a one-way transfer of the people that we have trained," the president said. "Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a life abroad. We ask only that those recruit our nurses, our teachers invest in the systems that recruited them."

Lalabalavu also alluded to Fiji recently declaring a national HIV emergency and said that organized crime and drug trafficking was exacerbating this problem. He said that as a small impoverished country, Fiji had three requests for the international community:

"That treatment and diagnostics reach small states at prices we can pay. That the Global Fund and UNAIDS be resources at a level that does not force triage between regions, and that our partners treat Pacific narcotics interdiction as the shared security interest it is."

Skip next section Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'

Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'

The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.

"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged. 

"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.

"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.

He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York." 

Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."

Skip next section Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago

Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was. 

"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."

Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."

Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.

Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.

Skip next section Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters

Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters

As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.

Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.

"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.

He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.

"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."

Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.

Skip next section READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.

Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.

"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.

Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.

Skip next section Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.

He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.

Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."

He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.

This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.

All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."

Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.

Skip next section Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."

Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.

Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."

He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.

entries.title: Germany news: Parliament approves fuel tax cut
entries.summary: German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, students in many cities are set to protest against military conscription. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Parliament approves fuel tax cut

Published September 25, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, students in many cities are set to protest against military conscription. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A fuel tax cut passes Bundestag as Germany faces high gas prices
  • A state minister reportedly pushes plan to limit asylum right
  • Students across Germany go on strike against potential return of military conscription

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Pistorius visits Budapest, plans 'restart' of military cooperation with Magyar government

Pistorius visits Budapest, plans 'restart' of military cooperation with Magyar government

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is in Hungary, announcing plans to reboot military cooperation with the EU and NATO member in light of this year's change of government. 

"Berlin and Budapest are growing politically closer together again," Pistorius said alongside his counterpart Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi in Budapest.

"This is a restart of relations between our countries, and that in turn is excellent new for our countries, for our people, but also for the entire NATO alliance and the European Union," he said.

Hungary's previous government under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban was perceived as unusually friendly towards Russia, certainly by NATO and EU standards, and critical of its neighbor Ukraine. 

New Prime Minister Peter Magyar has campaigned on seeking a reset to ties with Brussels, Kyiv and NATO. 

Defense Minister Ruszin-Szendi said, "We will be allies again. We will act as is expected of us and as we expect of our allies."

During his visit, Pistorius also went to Europe's largest synagogue, the Dohany Street Synagogue or Great Synagogue in Budapest.

Skip next section New law will make e-scooter companies liable for accidents, rather than renters

New law will make e-scooter companies liable for accidents, rather than renters

Companies renting out e-scoooters to the public will in future be liable for accidents involving the vehicles. 

A new law to this end passed the Bundesrat upper house of parliament on Friday. 

The idea is to make it easier for victims or people negatively affected by e-scooter crashes to claim compensation.

At present, the people renting the scooters are liable for accidents. Quite often these are minors, who should be covered by their parents' or guardian's general liability insurance — something all German residents are obliged to procure.

While any user of the rented scooter should therefore be covered, in practice it can often be prohibitively difficult or time-consuming to track them down and coordinate a claim.

The law will also apply to grey areas where it can be even more difficult to identify a responsible E-scooter user. For instance, as well as crashes, it would cover cases such as a pedestrian tripping and falling because of an E-scooter being parked or deposited in an illegal or dangerous place.

Until now, would-be claimants would have needed to demonstrate who had parked the scooter, which could be difficult or even impossible if companies allowed anonymized hiring and usage.

E-scooters are treated like bicycles, with less stringent insurance requirements than those for motorized vehicles which require bespoke personal insurance for legal road usage.

Skip next section READ: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany

READ: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany

Germany car making giant Volkswagen and its subidiary company Audi  are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to steering problems, according to media reports.

Skip next section Germany's Heidenau bans new Stolpersteine dedicated to victims of Holocaust

Germany's Heidenau bans new Stolpersteine dedicated to victims of Holocaust

The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on the public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to curb the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.

The city's administration urged against the motion. The initiators, however, argued that placing the plaques in the street leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims."  They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.

With the local branch of Friedrich Merz's CDU joining forces with the AfD to pass the motion, it has also raised questions about the political "firewall" against the far right pledged by mainstream German parties.

The International Auschwitz Committee described the CDU support as scandalous.

"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said the organization's Executive Vice President Christoph Heubner.

Skip next section Bundestag passes fuel tax rebate

Bundestag passes fuel tax rebate

Lawmakers in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house of parliament, approved a temporary cut to the fuel tax on Friday.

The government will ​cut ‌taxes on gas and diesel by about €0.17 per liter startig from October to the start of the new year in an effrot to help ​citizens cope with prices that have jumped since the Iran war.

It's the second time this year Germany has temporarily cut the fuel tax. The measure is expected to cost the federal and state governments €2.5 billion in lost tax revenue.

Skip next section Berlin can afford housing expropriations, German researchers say

Berlin can afford housing expropriations, German researchers say

Germany's socialist Left Party, which won the most votes at the recent Berlin election, is planning to tackle the city's housing crisis by expropriating large companies that own 3,000 or more apartments in the German capital. The plan has already triggered strong opposition from the federal level, including center-right Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has pledged there would be "no expropriation of private property in Germany."

A new study by economic researchers, including scholars from Germany's independent Macroeconomic Policy Institute (IMK), found that the Left's plan can be funded without breaking the bank.

The researchers found that Berlin can afford to expropriate around 210,000 apartments while paying some €13.5 billion in compensation to the corporate owners. The study, published on Friday, indicates such a move could be done without slowing down the construction of new homes or new budget cuts in the city-state.

The paper warns that expropriation would not solve the housing issues without widespread construction of new homes, but it adds that the move could be an additional element in tackling the affordability crisis.

Skip next section Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor, one of Germany's biggest airlines, will be fully owned by UK investor Attestor by the end of August next year.

The German federal government and the Hesse state government currently own nearly half of the company. The state authorities acquired their stake in 2021, after stepping in to help the carrier as it reeled from the pandemic-related travel disruptions and the 2019 bankruptcy of its UK parent company Thomas Cook.

The airline received state support totaling €930 million ($1.06 billion at the current exchange rate), which it fully paid off by March this year.

Skip next section Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Even with the summer officially over in Germany, the Rhine River, one of the country's essential trade routes, continues to dry up.

The latest data indicate that a gauge at Kaub, near the city of Koblenz, showed only 2 centimeters (less than an inch) of water on Thursday. This would make it the lowest value ever recorded since the measurement began in 1856.

By Friday, it had somewhat recovered to reach 5 centimeters.

It is important to note that these values show the water depth only at the gauge point, which is located relatively close to the shore. The actual navigable depth at Kaub is around 113 centimeters deeper than what's shown at the measuring point.

However, German shipping associations use the gauge value as a reference. Previously, the German Inland Waterways Association (BDB) stated that the Rhine is no longer fully navigable if the gauge values drop into single digits.

Any interruption of Rhine commercial traffic carries major economic risks for Germany. Many businesses use the river as a shipping lane connecting them to large North Sea harbors. In 2023, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

Skip next section Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

A four-point plan by conservative Saxon state Interior Minister Armin Schuster aims to limit the right to asylum by changing the European Convention on Human Rights and likely the German constitution, known as the Basic Law, according to multiple media reports.

The minister's plan, seen by the DPA news agency and Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland, says the German cities' and municipalities' ability to cope with asylum-seekers should determine how many are allowed in the country, rather than the current law that grants the right to asylum to anyone persecuted on political grounds.

Schuster's initiative would also see rejected asylum-seekers taken into custody in order to ensure deportation.

Germany's laws would be amended to allow a "deportation mandate."

"In order to fully implement the shift in migration policy, we need to ensure deportation for people who are ordered to leave, including criminals and those who do not integrate," Schuster said.

Skip next section Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Over 100 protests are expected across Germany as students push back on what they believe to be government's efforts to reintroduce military conscription.

The idea has been floated by senior politicians, including a former defense minister and the current premier of Bavaria earlier this month.

Germany has seen several waves of protests against the idea in recent years.

The immediate trigger for the school strike on Friday, however, is the military testing drive for young men in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein. According to protest organizers, authorities are calling for men born in 2008 to be tested even if they have previously declared no interest in serving in the military.

A spokeswoman for the German Defense Ministry confirmed that the examination is mandatory regardless of the teenagers' stated preferences, though the policy has not yet been implemented all over the country.

Germany suspended mandatory military conscription in 2011.

Skip next section German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

With oil prices still high on global markets, the German government is cutting the tax on gas and diesel at the gas station, with the move expected to pass the federal parliament later on Friday.

In order to save time, the government has attached the legal changes to a different law. If the measure is passed, it will save German drivers up to 16.7 euro cents per liter (about $0.72 per US gallon) from October 1.

The ADAC motoring association reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high last week, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 unleaded and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively).

Gas stations are not obligated to pass the full savings to the customers. However, a similar tax cut introduced earlier this year showed a strong effect on gas prices in May and June.

The measure is expected to stay in effect until the end of the year.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A schönen guten Morgen from DW's news team in Bonn! It is indeed a beautiful, sunny morning in Germany, and good news may be coming — at least for drivers looking to save money at the gas station.

Later today, the country's parliament will vote on a tax cut that should save customers up to 16.7 euro cents per liter (about $0.72 per US gallon), due to go into effect on October 1.

In more somber news, many schools across the country are expected to protest against what they see as the government's push to bring back military conscription.

We will be bringing you updates on these and other top news stories from Germany throughout the day.

entries.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
entries.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

"I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.

Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.

Russian influence impacting democratization efforts

Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow. 

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were  pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.

Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."

The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.

Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.

Freedom of expression under threat

Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

Artists have generally been playing a powerful role in the protests: "There were many actions that were very artistically conceived," Lapauri-Burk noted.

"Ode to Joy" from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony — the official anthem of the European Union — has often been played as a pro-European symbol of democratic resistance at anti-government protests in Tbilisi, Georgia, Rescheto added.

DW's new Georgian-language service

This year, Georgia is the focus of the Beethovenfest's Campus Project; a cultural exchange project developed in cooperation with DW. 

"Music transcends borders and language barriers and brings people together," DW's director general Barbara Massing noted at the opening of the panel discussion, which also celebrated the recent launch of DW's new Georgian-language service on Instagram. Georgian has now become Deutsche Welle's 33rd language.

"With the new Georgian-language service in cooperation with France Medias Monde and TVP World, we are strengthening the European commitment to free media and trustworthy information in a region that is specifically targeted by disinformation campaigns and faces unique political and social challenges," said Massing.

Robakidze welcomes such an initiation supporting Georgians who still hope for a democratic future. Severe fatigue, state crackdowns and a sense of despair among participants is seeing protest dwindling. Even so, "We still need to remain ready to take action," she said. To that end, "We need all the media support we can get."

Edited by: Hans Kellett

entries.title: Xi wraps up US visit with trip to National Archives
entries.summary: On the last day of his visit to the US, Chinese leader Xi Jinping will visit the National Archives with President Donald Trump, where the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution are stored. DW has more.
entries.content:
United States of America

Xi wraps up US visit with trip to National Archives

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

On the last day of his visit to the US, Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the National Archives with President Donald Trump, where the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution are stored. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • On the last day of Xi Jinping's visit, he and Donald Trump, along with their spouses, had tea at the White House.
  • Trump praised the progress he and Xi had made during Xi's visit to the US.
  • Xi said he expected two more meetings with Trump this year.
  • Trump and Xi visited the National Archives after the tea session.
  • On Thursday, following the talks, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping and their wives attended a state dinner hosted in honor of the Chinese leader.

Follow along here for live updates on Xi's state visit to the US:

Skip next section Trump confirms he discussed Iran war with Xi

Trump confirms he discussed Iran war with Xi

US President Donald Trump said he discussed the Iran war with his visiting Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.

When asked if they had discussed Iran, Trump replied, "We did," as he showed Xi around the National Archives in Washington.

Trump was also asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. He replied, "I think we're going to do great."

Skip next section Xi says he expects to meet with Trump 2 more times this year

Xi says he expects to meet with Trump 2 more times this year

Meanwhile, Chinese President Xi Jinping suggested the possibility of two more meetings with US President Donald Trump this year.

"Looking ahead to the remainder of this year, there will be two more opportunities for us to meet each other — firstly the APEC meeting in China and then the G20 summit in the United States," Xi said through a translator at the White House.

"I do welcome you, Mr President and the First Lady, to visit China," he added.

Trump responded, “We will, and we’ll be speaking a lot.”

Xi also said that the US-China relationship will be one of strategic stability based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. He went on to say that he and Trump had agreed to add new substance to this relationship.

Skip next section Trump says he and Xi made 'tremendous strides'

Trump says he and Xi made 'tremendous strides'

President Donald Trump praised the progress he and Chinese leader Xi  Jinping had made during Xi's visit to the US.

"I think we've made tremendous strides, we've made great strides, very positive for both countries," Trump told journalists while he and his wife, Melania, were having tea with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the White House.

Trump also added that the two sides will "be speaking a lot."

Skip next section US to reveal details on China trade talks on Monday

US to reveal details on China trade talks on Monday

The United States is expected to release details on the outcome of trade negotiations with China on Monday, according to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

"We're in a managed trade situation ... ​we've had progress, and we will release on Monday, I think, a lot ​more details about what we've accomplished over the past ​few weeks ‌in negotiating with the Chinese," he told CNBC on Friday.

Greer also said that the US has agreed with China to exempt some key goods from trade disputes.

He added that the US would export agricultural products and medical devices, and import consumer goods and other "non-sensitive" items from China.

Greer also mentioned that the current talks did not cover a small amount of high-quality, US-made chips that require licenses.

Last April, the US increased import tariffs on Chinese goods in several stages, raising them to up to 145%. In response, China imposed counter-tariffs of up to 125% and restricted exports of certain materials.

The two sides later agreed to several 90-day suspensions of new tariffs before Trump and Xi reached a broader trade agreement in South Korea last October. The deal was set to expire in November.

Skip next section Xi wraps up US visit with tea and trip to National Archives

Xi wraps up US visit with tea and trip to National Archives

On the final day of Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the US, he and President Donald Trump, along with their spouses, are back at the White House for a tea session.

Then, the two leaders are scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the Bill of Rights are kept.

After the tour, Xi is expected to leave Washington.

On Thursday, Trump and Xi met for talks at the White House, followed by a state dinner later in the day.

However, DW's analysis shows that little progress was made at the summit on key issues of US-Chinese relations, such as trade tensions and AI regulation. 

Skip next section What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far

What you need to know about Xi's meeting with Trump in Washington so far

US President Donald Trump on Thursday rolled out the red carpet for China's Xi Jinping on the Chinese president's first state visit to Washington in over a decade.

Ahead of the meeting, Xi said the US and China "should be partners rather than rivals," while Trump hailed his "truly great friendship" with the Chinese president. However, no breakthrough was expected in the trade tensions between the world's two largest economies.

The talks centered on the Middle East, Ukraine and the Korean Peninsula, according to a statement by Beijing. The US has not provided details about the meeting.

After the talks, Xi attended a lavish state dinner with Trump and US tech executives, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and Tesla's Elon Musk.

Trump described the event as the "hottest ticket in town" and said the "entire tech world" and "entire banking world and a lot more" would attend.

On Friday, Xi is scheduled to visit the National Archives, where the US Declaration of Independence, Constitution and Bill of Rights are held.

Skip next section Protesters gather in downtown Washington to protest Xi's visit

Protesters gather in downtown Washington to protest Xi's visit

A few hundred protesters gathered near the White House to rally against Xi Jinping's visit to the US.

Protesters highlighted a number of issues, from calls for religious freedom and autonomy in Tibet, Hong Kong and the Xinjiang region to demands that China refrain from interfering in Taiwan.

Protesters gathered in Lafayette Park, north of the White House, while other groups gathered outside the Chinese embassy. Pro-Xi rallies were also held in Washington.

Skip next section Trump says he and Xi have 'never gotten along better' at dinner toast

Trump says he and Xi have 'never gotten along better' at dinner toast

US President Donald Trump continued to heap praise on his guest, Chinese President Xi Jinping, during a White House state dinner on Thursday.

"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."

"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.

Earlier discussions between Xi and Trump touched on tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence.

Skip next section State dinner includes tech-heavy guest list, but Chinese CEOs are missing

State dinner includes tech-heavy guest list, but Chinese CEOs are missing

Apart from the heads of state and their spouses, the list of invitees to the state dinner included a host of big tech names.

Industry titans including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman, and Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell were all in attendance.

If this sounds familiar, it's because a similar group of tech leaders also accompanied Trump on his state visit to China in May. Names such as Nvidia's Jensen Huang, former Apple CEO Tim Cook, and once again Musk, were hosted by the Chinese president at a state dinner in the Great Hall of the People.

But Chinese CEOs are conspicuously missing on the guest list this evening in Washington as bringing Chinese firms to the US may raise more questions than it answers, experts said.

The Associated Press reported that US and Chinese planners did discuss including notable Chinese companies, but that one obstacle was that the US side was slow to suggest protocols and what roles the Chinese CEOs would have in the state visit.

Just like on Thursday, despite the star-studded business attendance, few major deals were announced during Trump's visit to China.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Trump hosts Xi at black-tie state dinner

IN PICTURES: Trump hosts Xi at black-tie state dinner

Skip next section What's on the menu at Trump's state dinner for Xi?

What's on the menu at Trump's state dinner for Xi?

Attention has now turned to the state dinner, a lighter-hearted event where everything from meal choices to seating arrangements will nevertheless be scrutinized for potential diplomatic intel.

"Everyone wants to be there," Trump said at the UN General Assembly. "It's the hottest ticket in town."

To start, the leaders and guests will dine on yellow squash veloute with wild mushrooms, fresh herbs, crispy pancetta and drizzled scallion oil.

The main course will be sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte.

For dessert, the guests will be treated to vanilla cremeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House bee hives.

The guest list includes Silicon Valley titans like Apple's Tim Cook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Alphabet's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.

"I would say you have the entire tech world, the entire banking world and a lot more," Trump told reporters earlier in the week.

Skip next section US, Iran should return to talks under memorandum of understanding, Xi says

US, Iran should return to talks under memorandum of understanding, Xi says

Chinese leader Xi Jinping said he supported the US and Iran's memorandum of understanding to end the Iran war, Xinhua state agency reported.

Xi said he expressed hope that the US and Iran would return to resolving issues through dialogue and negotiation under the agreement as soon as possible.

Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have held lengthy indirect talks with Iranian officials during the UN gathering earlier this week.

US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a phased path out of the war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, Reuters reported.

Skip next section Melania Trump, Madame Peng head to Asian art museum

Melania Trump, Madame Peng head to Asian art museum

First Lady Melania Trump and Xi's wife Peng Liyuan left their husbands behind to tour one of the largest Asian art museums in the US.

The visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art in Washington was supposed to celebrate cultural ties between the US and China.

Both wives are known for their focus on soft power and cultural issues, one is a former fashion model and the other a soprano.

A choir of young school children from the Hope Chinese School sang to the duo as they toured the building, singing famous Chinese folk songs including "Song and Smile" and "Jasmine Flower."

It's the first public meeting between the two spouses in nearly a decade, since a 2017 encounter in Beijing. A crowd had gathered on the sidewalk across from the museum, some waving Chinese and American flags.

Skip next section Trump says the pair had a 'great meeting,' takes Xi inside presidential helicopter

Trump says the pair had a 'great meeting,' takes Xi inside presidential helicopter

Trump's first comments to reporters after the talks were brief in the extreme.

In response to shouted questions as he took Xi to board the Marine One presidential helicopter for a brief tour, he told reporters, "We had a great meeting."

Images from the meeting showed that Chinese Vice Premier Hi Lifeng and Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended at least part of the talks, as did US Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Xi left the White House after the meeting, but will be back later for the state dinner.

Skip next section Xi tells Trump China's position on Taiwan and territory is 'crystal clear'

Xi tells Trump China's position on Taiwan and territory is 'crystal clear'

China's Xinhua news agency is reporting comments it says Xi Jinping relayed to Donald Trump during their talks in the Oval Office. 

Xi said he hoped the United States would continue to oppose "Taiwan independence" and handle the question of Taiwan with "prudence," according to Xinhua.

He reportedly told the US president that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was "crystal clear."

The US holds a complicated position when it comes to Taiwan. On the one hand, it is the small island nation's most important security guarantor. However, it has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan and does not recognize it as an independent country as part of its adherence to the so-called "one China" principle Beijing insists upon from all partners.

Xi also reportedly told Trump that China would support the US and Iran returning to negotiations "as soon as possible" as their naval standoff in the Persian Gulf drags well past the six-month mark.

entries.title: AfD, CDU ban new Holocaust 'stumbling stones' in Heidenau
entries.summary: Activists, politicians and representatives of Holocaust victims reacted with anger after the center-right CDU party joined forces with the AfD to ban new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) in the eastern town of Heidenau.
entries.content:
Germany

AfD, CDU ban new Holocaust 'stumbling stones' in Heidenau

September 25, 2026

Activists, politicians and representatives of Holocaust victims reacted with anger after the center-right CDU party joined forces with the AfD to ban new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) in the eastern town of Heidenau.

The town of Heidenau, near Dresden, has banned new Stolpersteine (stumbling stones) on public streets, with the center-right CDU and the far-right AfD voting together to stop the installation of new memorial plaques bearing the names of Holocaust victims.

The Stolpersteine are comprised of a concrete cube with a metal plaque on top that bears the victim's name. They are often seen in German streets, installed just slightly higher than the surrounding walking surface, often near the houses of people targeted by the Nazi regime.

German artist Gunter Demnig started the project in the early 1990s. While most of the 128,000 such paving stones were installed in Germany, they have also been placed in 30 other countries affected by the Nazi regime, making them the largest decentralized monument in the world.

Creator of Stolpersteine pledges to keep on working

The initiators of the Heidenau ban argue that, while remembering Holocaust victims is an essential task, the placement of stones leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring Holocaust victims at one of the city's cemeteries instead.

Demnig, now 78, has rejected this argument. The artist said that remembrance must be visible where people used to live, and that stumbling stones make history tangible for local young people. At the same time, he said he saw the ban coming due to the outcome of recent state elections in Germany.

"After the electoral successes of the AfD, something like this was completely expected," Demnig was quoted as saying by the DPA news agency. He expressed hope that the Heidenau ban would remain an exception and pledged to "push on now more than ever" with his work.

Demnig also accused the center-right CDU (Christian Democratic Union) of abandoning Christian values. He said the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz "should maybe drop the C" from their acronym "because they have dropped Christianity already."

CDU's support of AfD in Heidenau 'a scandal'

Many others also responded with outrage to the CDU's decision to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion. The move comes with Chancellor Merz already facing a political crisis over his party's poor electoral performance, and raises questions about the political "firewall" against the far right which mainstream political parties in Germany have maintained to keep the AfD out of power.

On Friday, one of the top two leaders of Germany's Green Party, Felix Banaszak, described the move as "a scandal."

Banaszak pointed to the current debate on right-wing extremism and the rise of the AfD, saying that everything must be done "to keep alive the memories of those who were persecuted and killed."

The International Auschwitz Committee also slammed the CDU support to the motion as scandalous.

"This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery," said Christoph Heubner, the organization's executive vice president.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
entries.summary: In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure security.
entries.content:
Lithuania

Lithuanian prime minister urges stronger NATO air defense

September 25, 2026

In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure security.

Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.

The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.

For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.

"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.

"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."

Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond

Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.

Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.

"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."

For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.

National security climbs national agenda

Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.

"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."

But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.

For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.

The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.

Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.

'We will continue to support Ukraine'

Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.

The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.

"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.

Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.

"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."

Edited by: Jess Smee

entries.title: India news: Protests against election chief escalate as Gandhi, Cockroach party allege 'rigged' vote
entries.summary: Police have used tear gas on protests by the opposition Congress party demanding India's election commission head steps down, following a report alleging "rigged" elections. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Protests over 'rigged' elections escalate

Published September 25, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

Police have used tear gas on protests by the opposition Congress party demanding India's election commission head steps down, following a report alleging "rigged" elections. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Here are some of the major headlines from India on Friday, September 25:

  • Police detain protesters at Jantar Mantar rally against election chief
  • Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement have labelled India’s elections "rigged"
  • Gandhi and the CJP have claimed voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP
  • Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few
  • Another incident of harassment of minor girl surfaces in Bihar

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Thanks for reading!

Thanks for reading!

That is all for today! There will be more updates tomorrow.

Here is another terrible haiku to bridge that gap:

Voting is a right,

Till it is not anymore,

Reading news is good.

 

Skip next section Election chief under pressure as protests escalate

Election chief under pressure as protests escalate

Protesters from various groups gathered in Delhi on Friday demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, amid a growing controversy over reported differences within the Election Commission of India (ECI).



The protest followed an investigation published by The Indian Express on September 23, which reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally raised objections at least 14 times over a 10-month period to decisions concerning electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The report said some of the decisions had been taken without their knowledge.



The Election Commission, however, has rejected the suggestion of an internal breakdown, saying that differences expressed through internal notes are part of the normal decision-making process and that the final decisions of the three-member Commission were unanimous. 



On Thursday, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) gave Gyanesh Kumar 48 hours to resign and warned that it would launch a nationwide agitation, including a second protest at Jantar Mantar, if he did not step down. 



On Friday, CPI(ML) Liberation leader Dipankar Bhattacharya, AISA leader Neha Bora — who had gone on hunger strike during the first Jantar Mantar protest — senior advocate Prashant Bhushan and activist Yogendra Yadav joined the demonstration.



The Delhi Police had heavily barricaded the area around Jantar Mantar and did not allow protesters to enter the designated protest site. Several activists were detained within minutes of arriving at the spot.



Speaking to DW, Neha Bora accused the Election Commission of “stealing votes” and acting against democracy. She demanded Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and said the protesters would continue their movement.



Dipankar Bhattacharya told DW that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) should be scrapped and that fresh elections should be held in several states.

Skip next section Police detain protesters at Jantar Mantar rally against election chief

Police detain protesters at Jantar Mantar rally against election chief

A protest called by left-wing student group All India Students' Association (AISA) and others at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Friday against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was met with a heavy police presence. 

Reports said several protesters, including AISA president Neha Bora, were detained.

Earlier, Bora had said the protest would demand the resignation of Kumar and will be "defending our democracy."

Police heavily cordoned off the protest site, preventing people from entering and barring protesters from approaching within about 100 meters, according to a DW correspondent.

Kumar has faced criticism over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists. The Election Commission says the exercise aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Critics allege it has also removed eligible voters and benefited the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Skip next section US citizen Matthew VanDyke granted bail, allowed to travel back

US citizen Matthew VanDyke granted bail, allowed to travel back

Self-professed US mercenary Matthew VanDyke and a Ukrainian national were released from Delhi's Tihar jail on Thursday to travel to their respective countries despite being initially booked under India's stringent Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA), media reports said.

The two were allowed to travel to their respective countries for a month to meet their families, subject to court conditions, authorities said.

They were among seven foreign nationals arrested by India's National Investigation Agency (NIA) over alleged involvement in a drone-warfare training camp linked to ethnic armed groups in Myanmar.

All seven, including five other Ukrainian nationals, have been granted default bail and allowed to travel to Ukraine and the US.

The NIA had initially charged the group under UAPA, alleging they entered India legally but traveled to the northeast without required permits before crossing into Myanmar.

The agency later dropped terrorism-related UAPA provisions in its chargesheet, saying it lacked direct evidence that the alleged activities harmed India's sovereignty or citizens.

The accused were granted default bail after the NIA failed to complete its investigation within the mandatory 180-day period.

VanDyke describes himself as an international security analyst and founder of Sons of Liberty International. He also directed a film about the war in Syria.

Skip next section Another incident of harassment of minor girl surfaces in Bihar

Another incident of harassment of minor girl surfaces in Bihar

Yet another incident where a minor girl was harassed in public in Bihar has surfaced.

A social media video allegedly showed a minor girl being harassed at the Mandar Parvat tourist site in Banka in the eastern state.

Authorities said on Friday they have lodged a case against six unidentified youths after a video emerged that appears to show several young men attacking the girl. Police suspect the footage may be around six months old.

Police are investigating when the incident occurred and trying to identify those seen in the video.

The case comes days after a separate video allegedly showing a minor girl along with her male friend being harassed in Samastipur in Bihar led to the arrest of four people.

Skip next section Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few

Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few

The Election Commission of India (ECI) introduced a "Mark VIP" feature in an app used by local election officials during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists, the Hindustan Times newspaper reported.

VIP denotes a Very Important Person.

The feature was added to the BLO App on July 30, according to officials in Delhi's chief electoral officer's office, the newspaper reported. Apple's App Store records described the update as "mark VIP elector related changes."

The ECI did not respond to questions about the feature or the legal basis for its introduction, the report said.

A separate investigation by The Reporters' Collective found that election officials had been instructed to mark ministers, judges, bureaucrats, celebrities and other prominent figures as VIPs during the revision. It reported that such voters could receive preferential treatment, including avoiding hearings required of ordinary voters.

In recent days, Delhi's chief electoral officer has issued notices to nearly 3.3 million voters during the SIR exercise, which included Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and Foreign Minister S Jaishankar.

Skip next section Cockroach party urges opposition to boycott India's 'rigged' elections

Cockroach party urges opposition to boycott India's 'rigged' elections

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday called on India's opposition parties to stop participating in India's "rigged" elections, as it threatened to launch protests across the country on October 2.

"For opposition: Yes, elections are being rigged," Dipke posted on social media, arguing that if the opposition continues to contest such elections, it legitimizes them and "maintain the illusion that they are free and fair."

"If elections are being rigged, it should matter regardless of the state or which party is affected," Dipke wrote, calling on opposition parties to prioritize democracy over political survival. "You cannot keep saying the game is rigged while continuing to play it. Your participation is the only thing that gives these rigged elections legitimacy."

On Thursday, the CJP accused India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy and demanded his resignation within 48 hours.

CJP alleged that the Election Commission's voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The CJP's demands include:

  • Criminal proceedings against Kumar
  • All upcoming elections put on hold, freeze Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
  • Repeal the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India

Meanwhile, two petitions were filed in the Bombay High Court on Thursday challenging the SIR process in Maharashtra.

Skip next section Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'

Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'

Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement called India’s elections "rigged," as the uproar over the Election Commission of India's (ECI) handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of abating.

On Thursday, Congress Party leader Gandhi alleged that elections in India were being "rigged," and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. It followed a report by Indian Express on objections raised by two election commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.

The report said that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions on voter registrations and electoral data. In one instance, one of the complaints said the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The three commissioners are overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which the ECI says aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Critics say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters, which has benefitted the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"If the vote has been destroyed, then our Constitution has been destroyed. It no longer has power," Gandhi said during a press conference.

Gandhi also alleged that Kumar was elevated to Election Commission head by Prime Minster Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, despite his opposition to the appointment. He went on to accuse them of being "at the top of the conspiracy," and called for them to be investigated.

Meanwhile, BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi defended the ECI, saying on Thursday that the SIR process was legally sound and that the commission’s decisions were based on majority consensus. He said the law empowers the ECI to conduct an SIR at its discretion.

India's next general elections are not expected until 2029, but a series of important state elections will take place next year.
