The furor over the Indian Express investigation that thrust the Election Commission of India (ECI) into the spotlight over its handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of dying down. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and satirical political movement, the Cockroach Party, have both described India's elections as "rigged." The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), however, has rallied in support of the ECI.

Staying with the ECI, it turns out there are citizens who are more equal than others, as the voter-list revision now sees some names marked VIP — Very Important Person. The list is said to include elected representatives, judges, holders of constitutional or other declared offices, and prominent figures from the arts and culture.

Meanwhile, another day and another case of alleged sexual assault in public, a video has surfaced purportedly showing a minor girl being harassed in Bihar again.

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival
entries.summary: The pope has landed in Paris for a four-day trip. Received by President Emmanuel Macron, Leo warned about the risks of AI and criticized France's limited legalization of assisted dying.
entries.content:
France

Pope Leo XIV criticizes AI, assisted dying on France arrival

September 25, 2026

The pope has landed in Paris for a four-day trip. Received by President Emmanuel Macron, Leo warned about the risks of AI and criticized France's limited legalization of assisted dying.

Pope Leo XIV arrived for a four-day visit to France on Friday, the first official papal visit to the strictly secular country in 18 years.

Leo, the spiritual leader of the some 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide, was greeted at Paris' Orly Airport by French President Emmanuel Macron and will be in the country until Monday.

What did Pope Leo say alongside Macron at the Elysee Palace?

In remarks delivered at the Elysee Palace, Leo on Friday underscored opposition to assisted dying initiatives just two months after France created a legal right ‌to ⁠die ⁠for those with incurable illnesses.

Though he did ​not specifically mention France's new law, the pontiff criticized ​what ‌he called "profit-driven ventures" such as surrogacy and assisted dying.

"I firmly reiterate that the protection ‌of ​the right to life constitutes the indispensable foundation of every other human right," the pope said in an address to Macron and other French politicians.

"I am concerned at times by those trends ⁠in ​society that risk turning science and ​technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the ​trade in human organs ‌or the possibility of arranging one's own death," he said.

Pope Leo also delivered an urgent warning regarding the development of artificial intelligence.

"If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a 'paradise of machines' invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for education in ethical discernment," he said.

What else in on the pope's itinerary in France?

The papal itinerary has Leo meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace, speaking at UNESCO headquarters, leading Vespers at Notre Dame Cathedral and celebrating Mass for an estimated 80,000 young people at the Stade de France national stadium on Friday.

On Saturday, he is scheduled to celebrate Mass for another 600,000 at Place de la Concorde on the Avenue des Champs-Elysees before departing for Lourdes, a famous Catholic pilgrimage site located near France's Spanish border.

On Monday, Leo will travel to Metz, near the German border, where he will deliver a speech entitled: "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity." Macron will introduce Leo at the event and has invited fellow leaders across the EU to join him in attendance.

Pope speaks of press freedom, peace on flight amid White House exclusion furor

While traveling to France, US-born Leo was asked by a CNN reporter for his thoughts on US President Donald Trump's attempts to ban news outlets from covering him.

"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he told reporters.

Leo, who was forced to fly home alone after plane trouble on a recent trip to Spain, took the opportunity to apologize to his press pool.

Speaking to reporters at the back of his plane on Friday, Leo said, "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn't have the flight back together back to Rome."

He further told reporters he was coming to France as "a pilgrim for peace" in a time of war.

Leo, a tireless critic of the wars in Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere, said "It is a message which at this time, as we all may know, is particularly important."

AI, Church sexual abuse also on the agenda

Leo had already tipped his hat on his plans to address global concerns regarding so-called artificial intelligence (AI) and the "new dangers" it presents to "security and international peace" during his discussions with Macron.

Speaking at the Vatican prior to departure on Thursday, Leo had said leaders must "govern wisely" when dealing with the new technology, which he says raises questions about the very essence of what it means to be human.

Leo has taken a keen interest in AI, writing his first papal encyclical — published this May and entitled "Magnificent Humanity" — on the issue.

The pope is also seeking to repair the Catholic Church's standing in France, where opinions grew particularly bleak in 2021 following the publication of a report documenting seven decades of abuse — impacting 330,000 French children — by clergy and lay leaders.

Leo will meet victims of church abuse during the trip.

entries.title: Bundesliga and three other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
entries.summary: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have called for major reforms to the world-governing body FIFA. However, they stopped short of calling for FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's resignation.
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have called for major reforms to the world-governing body FIFA. However, they stopped short of calling for FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's resignation.

The letter released this Friday and signed by the heads of the Bundesliga, The Premier League, La Liga, and Serie A called for major changes to how FIFA operates – and for a greater say in decision-making.

"Football's ​longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ​ideas rather than safeguarding against them," it said.

FFE private investment plan dropped

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has been facing a wave of criticism since late July, when his plan for private investment through a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), emerged. The idea was for FFE to organize FIFA's tournaments while maximizing profits.

Vigorous opposition from UEFA, European football's governing body, as well as CONCACAF (North and Central America plus the Caribbean) and the Asian Football Confederation led Infantino to quickly drop the plan.

However, the league bosses noted that this had not solved a deeper problem and appeared to dismiss a recent announcment by Infantino of an independent external review of FIFA governance as well as consultations on strengthening decision-making processes,.

'Fundamental governance reform essential'

"It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference," Friday's letter from the leagues said.

The last line was in reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker's one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium. While the ban was imposed by FIFA's disciplinary committee, it came after US President Donald Trump had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban – something Trump publicly admitted.

The leagues on Friday called for greater checks and balances to be implemented at FIFA, while at the same time demanding that they and others be given a say in decisions such as increases in the number of international matches.

Stakeholders 'not meaningfully involved in process'

"… when FIFA takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us – for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause – the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process," they said.

"A FIFA governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."

The letter, while implying much criticism of Infantino did not call for him to step down – it didn't even mention him by name.

Search for a challenger ongoing

This comes as UEFA has said it is looking for a suitable candidate to challenge Infantino in the next presidential election next March, in which Infantino has said he will run for reelection. UEFA has also called for an independent external review of how the FFE plan was developed and filed legal applications through the US courts for the disclosure of documents related to the plan. This was with a view to a possible criminal complaint being lodged in Switzerland if it is established that Infantino undervalued FFE at $20 billion (€17.5 billion).

FIFA has described UEFA's legal moves as a "smear campaign" against it but has not yet commented on Friday's letter from the league bosses.

Infantino aims to discuss his proposals at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on October 15, a week after UEFA is to hold a meeting of all of its 55 member associations on October 8 in Berlin.

Any person aiming to challenge Infantino in the March 18, 2027 FIFA presidential election must register as a candidate by November 18.

Edited by: Hecko Flores

entries.title: Why Eritrea matters as fighting returns to Tigray
entries.summary: The US has removed key sanctions on Eritrea as Houthi attacks disrupt Red Sea shipping and fighting escalates in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Analysts say Eritrea's strategic value is growing.
entries.content:
Africa

Why Eritrea matters as fighting returns to Ethiopia's Tigray

September 25, 2026

The US has removed key sanctions on Eritrea as Houthi attacks disrupt Red Sea shipping and fighting escalates in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Analysts say Eritrea's strategic value is growing.

On September 23, fighting escalated dramatically in Ethiopia's Tigray region. Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and fighting spread into the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, according to reports.

Both sides accuse the other of starting the escalation. The renewed fighting poses a major challenge to the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement that ended the previous Tigray war.

This is where Eritrea becomes crucial. Martin Plaut, a British journalist specializing in the Horn of Africa, noted that the US needs Eritrea in the struggle to secure the Red Sea against the Houthis, an Iran-backed Shiite Muslim militia.

Plaut argues that removing sanctions gives new political weight to one of Africa's most repressive regimes.

As fighting resumes in Tigray, Eritrea could once again become a decisive military player. Plaut said that the current tensions had the potential of developing into a broader regional confrontation, which, he said, "is the most serious danger." 

In his view, US President Donald Trump's administration has already made a strategic calculation: "Trump has now mended fences with Eritrea and has lifted sanctions against Eritrea" in an effort to reduce the threat posed by the Houthis and secure the Red Sea.

A striking coincidence of timing

The escalation in Tigray came only days after Washington removed key Eritrean entities and individuals from its sanctions list.

On September 18, the United States allowed the national emergency underpinning its Ethiopia-related sanctions regime to expire. The Treasury Department subsequently removed a number of Eritrean individuals and entities from its sanctions list, including senior financial official Hagos Ghebrehiwet and the Red Sea Trading Corporation. The measures had originally been imposed in 2021 in connection with the Tigray war.

US officials have not described the move as an endorsement of Eritrea, nor has Washington publicly said that it struck a deal with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki. But it removes a layer of pressure on a government whose strategic importance has grown as security around the Red Sea deteriorates.

For Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration and a political analyst, the wider geopolitical context is crucial.

"It is happening at a time when the war on Iran is ongoing," he told DW. "The Strait of Hormuz has been blocked for some time, and now the Bab el-Mendeb on the Red Sea, where Eritrea is located, this may give Eritrea some advantage to establish a meaningful relationship with the US."

Why Eritrea matters

Eritrea controls a long coastline opposite Yemen. Its southern port of Assab lies close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important maritime chokepoints.

Moses Okello, a senior researcher at the Institute for Security Studies in Addis Ababa, says the regional context has fundamentally changed since the previous Tigray war.

"In 2020, the concern was the TPLF [Tigray People's Liberation Front] versus the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF)," he told DW. "Today, the entire Middle East is up in flames, and now the tensions in the Red Sea. So this changes the strategic value of not just the Eritrean coast, but the entire Red Sea waterway."

For Washington, cooperation — or at least non-hostility — from Eritrea can therefore be strategically valuable.

But the bargain carries risks.

Eritrea is one of the world's most authoritarian states, with no national elections since independence in 1993 and an extensive system of indefinite national service. Eritrean forces also fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the 2020-22 Tigray war.

And the economic impact of lifting sanctions may be more limited than the political symbolism suggests. "Lifting the sanctions may not make a huge difference on the ground," said Sayed. "Eritrea is not a trade hub [nor does it have] a well-established trading relationship with the outside world. It's actually a closed country."

Ethiopia heads back towards war

The latest fighting did not emerge from nowhere.

On September 21, seven Ethiopian armed and political groups announced an alliance aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. The coalition includes the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Some members were on opposing sides during the 2020-22 Tigray war.

It remains unclear how closely the alliance's members will coordinate militarily. The alliance brings together groups with very different histories that share opposition to the federal government.

Two days later, fighting escalated in Tigray. Tigrayan forces seized airports and fighting spread into neighboring regions. The TPLF says federal forces attacked first; Addis Ababa says the TPLF launched the offensive.

The renewed fighting has raised questions about the durability of the 2022 Pretoria agreement.

Could Eritrea intervene?

During the previous Tigray war, Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops. But relations between Afwerki and Abiy have since deteriorated sharply.

One major dispute concerns Ethiopia's demand for reliable access to the Red Sea. Landlocked since Eritrea's independence, Ethiopia regards maritime access as a strategic necessity. Eritrea insists on its sovereignty and has rejected any suggestion that Ethiopia could obtain access through coercion.

The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups in the new conflict. Eritrea denies such allegations.

There is currently no public evidence that the US sanctions decision was designed to encourage Eritrean military intervention in Ethiopia. Nor is it clear that Asmara has decided to enter the fighting.

But if the Tigray conflict intensifies, Eritrea could see a direct security interest in intervening. That would transform an Ethiopian conflict into a potentially interstate confrontation.

A regional conflict waiting to spread

The Horn of Africa is already exceptionally volatile.

Sudan remains at war. Somalia is unstable. Ethiopia and Egypt remain locked in a dispute over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are pursuing their own interests across the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. And the conflict in Yemen is directly connected to the security of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Okello sees the changing Middle East as an additional reason for urgent engagement. "There is no doubt that the conflict in the Middle East now puts a new contextual layer over that primary tension and increases the urgency to engage with both Eritrea and Addis Ababa to try and address this before it becomes a conflagration which makes addressing issues in the Red Sea a lot more difficult."

A new Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore not happen in isolation.

Plaut warns that regional alliances could interact in dangerous ways. "You have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces," he told DW. "This could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

That does not mean a general regional war is inevitable. Most governments involved have strong reasons to prevent an uncontrollable escalation. But the number of links between the region's conflicts is increasing.

Eritrea and shifting regional dynamics

For Eritrea's President Afwerki, the US decision is an opportunity.

The end of the sanctions removes one source of international pressure and may give Eritrea greater diplomatic room for maneuver. More importantly, Washington's renewed engagement with Asmara underscores the strategic value of Eritrea's Red Sea position.

The more important Eritrea becomes to US and regional security calculations, the greater the danger that strategic interests will overshadow concerns about its authoritarian system and past military interventions.

For Ethiopia, the immediate question is whether the renewed fighting can be stopped before it draws in Eritrea.

For Washington, the challenge is whether Eritrea can be engaged as a Red Sea security partner without giving Asmara greater freedom to destabilize its neighbors.

Eritrea has spent decades on the margins of international diplomacy. Its location on the Red Sea has long given it strategic significance.

With fighting again raging in Tigray, the Houthis threatening the Red Sea and Washington reopening its channel to Asmara, Eritrea could become one of the key players in the Horn of Africa's next chapter.

Ekinder Firew in Addis Ababa contributed to this report.

Edited by: Andreas Illmer
